items.title: QSA decode has no working kernel path on SM121 (GB10 / DGX Spark); Qwen3.8-Flash-Next unservable
items.body:
## Summary

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next cannot serve on DGX Spark (GB10, SM121). QSA decode has no working kernel path there: `_resolve_trtllm_sparse_decode()` rejects the arch because of the `is_sm100_supported()` gate, classic flash_attn (FA2) is not installed and has no Blackwell kernels anyway, so the resolver lands on the flash-attn-4 CuTe interface, which fails to compile for this GPU. Every launch config crashes at the first decode or during decode CUDA graph capture.

The gate is the only real problem. The flashinfer trtllm sparse decode kernel itself works on SM121. I verified it with the same shape used in #36556:

```
device: NVIDIA GB10 cap: (12, 1)
q=[1,24,256], kv=[2051,2,256], page 64, bf16
kernel ran, out shape: (1, 24, 256)
max_abs_diff vs reference: 4.70e-04
```

This is the SM121 sibling of #36531. #36556 fixes the same resolver for SM120 (RTX 5090). SM121 needs to be included.

## Environment

- 2x DGX Spark (GB10, SM121, 128 GB unified memory), TP=2 over ConnectX-7
- image `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` (sha256:64c58f100438), sglang 0.0.0.dev1+gd91c3682b, torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, flashinfer with `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache`
- model `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` @ 7b719225, `--mem-fraction-static 0.75`

## Crash

```
cutlass MLIRError: Operation creation failed:
error: unknown: expects `coord` and shape of view are weakly congruent,
but got '!cute.layout<"(?,?):(?{i64 div=8},1)">', '!cute.coord<"(_,_,?)">'
```

via `qwen_sparse_attn_backend.py flash_attn_varlen_func -> flash_attn/cute/interface.py:1028 _flash_attn_fwd -> cute.compile(...)`.

Reached from three call sites, so no launch flag avoids it:

1. decode CUDA graph capture (`capture_decode_graph`)
2. the MTP draft: `eagle_worker_v2.draft -> qwen4_exp_mtp.py -> qwen_sparse_attn_backend.forward_decode`
3. eager decode on the target itself: `hybrid_linear_attn_backend.forward_decode -> qwen_sparse_attn_backend._forward_paged_attention`

`--attention-backend triton` does not help because QSA calls flash_attn directly.

## What works once decode has a kernel

I ran the pair end to end with an interim SM-agnostic Triton fallback in `_resolve_flash_attn_varlen_func` (fused single-query flash decode over the packed varlen layout, verified against `qsa_sparse_attention_reference`, CUDA graph capturable including the spec path). llama-benchy, pp2048/tg128:

| depth | c1 no spec | c1 MTP (steps=3, draft=4) | c2 MTP |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 24.6 | 37.6 | 49.2 |
| 16384 | 24.3 | 41.4 | 52.9 |

Decode is flat in depth, so QSA behaves as designed on this hardware. Two observations that may be useful for the qwen4 branch:

- c1 decode on GB10 is memory bandwidth bound. A profile shows 52 percent of GPU time in cuBLAS bf16 gemv on the non expert weights. A 3.7x faster QSA kernel did not change end to end c1 at all, so the kernel choice matters for correctness and concurrency, not c1 throughput.
- `speculative_num_draft_tokens > 4` is rejected by the compress ratio guard, so draft depth caps early on this model.

## Fix

PR incoming from my fork: extend the resolver gate so SM120 and SM121 can take the flashinfer trtllm sparse decode path, keeping current behavior everywhere else. Happy to also contribute the Triton fallback as a last resort rung if you want coverage for archs where neither trtllm nor FA2 is available.

items.title: [RFC] KV Cache Compression API (KVTC, nvCOMP, ...)
items.body:
## Overview

This document proposes a small set of SGLang API changes that enable integration of various KV cache (MHA/MLA/SSM/...) compression algorithms, either on the L1-L2 or L2-L3 boundary. Compression lowers the cost of inference by allowing to store more caches for longer amount of time and/or more users, thus increasing cache hit rates and mitigating certain prefills.

```text
┌────────┐      ╔═══════════════╗      ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐
│   L1   │ ◄──► ║ Compression / ║ ◄──► │   L2   │ ◄──► │   L3   │
│        │      ║ Decompression ║      │        │      │        │
└────────┘      ╚═══════════════╝      └────────┘      └────────┘

┌────────┐      ┌────────┐      ╔═══════════════╗      ┌────────┐
│   L1   │ ◄──► │   L2   │ ◄──► ║ Compression / ║ ◄──► │   L3   │
│        │      │        │      ║ Decompression ║      │        │
└────────┘      └────────┘      ╚═══════════════╝      └────────┘
```
In this document:
- **L1** is the device KV-cache pool, usually in GPU memory.
- **L2** is the host KV-cache pool in CPU DRAM, typically pinned memory.
- **L3** is an external storage backend reached through a connector such as NIXL.
- **KV cache** refers to MHA (GQA) or MLA cache, unless otherwise stated.
- **KV codec** a KV cache compression/decompression method, that can be plugged to HiCache using the described API (subclass of extended `HostKVCache`).

The API is purposefully minimal, and pushes most of the responsibilities to implementation of the codec.
The reason for this is the ease of code maintenance for HiCache, and dynamically-changing landscape of compression methods.

## Method coverage

| Method                        | API Support | Device            |        Compression ratio | Lossless | Description                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------- | :---------: | ----------------- | -----------------------: | :------: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **KVTC**                      |  ✓          | CPU/GPU           | **~8–20×**, up to **40×+** in-domain | ✗ | Applies a calibrated transform, adaptive quantization, and entropy coding; reconstructs full KV tensors before reuse.      |
| **ANS/Bitcomp/... via nvCOMP**|  ✓          | GPU               | up to **1.25×** (roughly) | ✓ | NVIDIA numerical-data codec; the lossless mode compresses dense or sparse numeric tensors without reconstruction error.   |
| **DFloat11**/**SplitZip**/**ZipNN**     |  ✓          | GPU               | **1.35×**           | ✓ | Encodes common BF16 exponents with short codes while preserving signs, mantissas, and uncommon exponents exactly.          |
| **TurboQuant** (offload-only) |  ✓          | GPU               | **4—5×** | ✗ | Rotates and quantizes KV dims during offload, then reconstructs native-precision KV during reload.               |
| **KVCodec**                   |  ✓          | GPU + NVENC/NVDEC | **~10×** | ✗ | Rearranges and quantizes KV tensors into a codec-friendly format processed by GPU video-codec hardware.                    |
| **CacheGen**                  |  ✓          | CPU/GPU           | **3.5—4.3×** | ✗ | Uses layer- and token-aware quantization with entropy coding and selectable quality levels.                                |
| **Eviction** (H₂O, SnapKV, ...) | ✗         | GPU               | **Policy-dependent** | ✗ | Heuristically removes cache tokens considered no longer useful. Irreversible. |

## Crucial characteristics of KV cache compression methods

Below is a list of the most important characteristics that characterize a broad range of methods developed
to date, from the point of view of their implementation, runtime and integration into SGLang.

| Characteristic                                         | Description |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- |
| **Lossy or lossless**                                  | Lossy methods are prone to accumulation of compression errors over repeated recompression. |
| **On-the-fly or lazy**                                 | Methods which are too slow/too resource-hungry might require a queueing mechanism and additional buffers. |
| **CPU-based or GPU-based**                             | GPU-based methods interfere with LLM runtime, while CPU-based are less predictable in terms of available resources (available CPU cycles, interference with other processes, amd64/arm extended instruction sets). |
| **Predictable-size or variable-size blocks**           | Such data might complicate buffer allocation and cause conflicts with 3rd party L3 libraries. |
| **MQA, MLA, or SSM**                                   | More sophisticated methods are designed for specific kinds of cache. |
| **Attention-head axis dependencies**                   | If compression requires a number of heads or layers for compression, and a model is split across many accelerators, it might require gathering the caches across a number of ranks. |
| **Layer-axis dependencies**                            | In addition to possible required gathering over PP ranks, decompressing N layers at a time needs a mechanism beyond `load_to_device_per_layer`, which materializes exactly one layer per call. |
| **Time-axis dependencies**                             | A method compressing a number of consecutive time steps may additionally require information about position in context to undo RoPE for better compressibility. |
| **Additional artifacts on the GPU (e.g., PCA matrix)** | During runtime, the artifacts might take up space in memory and require offline preparation/calibration. |
| **Decompressed size different from the original**      | Common for token eviction methods. The compression API does not support this kind of methods due to the amount of issues which changing cache size causes. |
| **Relies on algorithms implemented in HW**             | NVIDIA Decompression Engine, HW video codecs, etc. |

### Lossy compression and the risk of error accumulation
Two cases should be considered separately:
 * **L1-L2 decompression**: By design, HiCache never offloads twice the same caches from L1. *Until this assumption holds, there is no risk of error accumulation*. This is enforced by the backuped/host_value protocol.
  Specifically, any pre-existing caches for a conversation that are being onloaded from L2 (or L3 through L2) onto L1, are retained on L2 during generation. When the generation is over, only the newly created caches, which correspond to the newly generated tokens, are offloaded to L2.
 * **L2-L3 decompression**: If a cache is retrieved from L3, decompressed and immediately evicted from L3, it may be re-compressed in the future during offloading L1->L2->L3.

### Lazy compression
Many classical codecs are asymmetric in terms of their latency: compression typically takes longer than decompression (e.g., due to codebook building). Methods not fit for compression on-the-fly (during offload, e.g., through zero copy) proceed as follows:
1. Offload the cache from L1 to L2.
2. Queue a compression request. At this point we task the codec with managing a compression queue.
3. Compress the cache to L2, retaining the original (uncompressed) cache in L2.
4. Delete the original cache and update pointers to cache (atomic).

This mode of operation puts an additional requirement on the `HostKVCache` to have an additional compression buffer in L2. In addition, if CPU is used for both compression/decompression, the codec is responsible for maintaining priorities of (de)compression requests, since decompression requests are on the critical path and should have absolute priority.

`HostKVCache` should be able to create CPU threads and CUDA streams for deferred compression.

In particular, a `HostKVCache` instance could transfer raw, uncompressed KV-cache data into a designated host, L2, buffer and schedule compression asynchronously in the background, either on a separate CUDA stream or on CPU.

When a load request is sent, the module can check whether the data is still present in the uncompressed buffer or has already been moved into the compressed region.

### GPU-based decompression
GPU decompression should run as part of the existing host-to-device load operation. A codec may copy the compressed payload to a GPU staging buffer and launch its decompression kernel from `load_to_device_per_layer()`. The kernel must use the CUDA stream that is current when the method is called, rather than launching implicitly on the default stream. In the current HiCache path, this is the existing `load_stream`; because the copy, decompression kernel, and per-layer completion event are ordered on the same stream, the model cannot read the destination KV-cache slots before decompression has completed. No additional codec-specific stream is therefore required.

A codec should create another stream only if it implements a separate copy/decompression pipeline; in that case, it must add explicit CUDA-event dependencies between the streams and preserve the lifetime of staging buffers and temporary tensors with `record_stream()` or equivalent synchronization.

Asynchronous host-to-device transfer also requires pinned host memory, and any GPU staging or scratch buffers must be included in the codec’s memory requirements. Running decompression on the load stream may overlap it with model execution, but overlap is not guaranteed and may reduce inference performance when decompression competes with model kernels for GPU compute or memory bandwidth.

### Across time/device dependencies
If the caches need to be gathered for compression across parallel ranks (TP/PP/..), and distributed across rank during decompression, it is a task of a particular codec. In particular, for MLA caches, a codec might benefit from GPU-based decompression in parallel on multiple ranks, even if the cache technically does not need to be gathered.

### Prefix caching
Keeping an uncompressed window of N recent tokens is widely used for improving the accuracy of lossy compression methods, since auto-regressive Transformer models attend more frequently to the latest tokens. However, this limits prefix caching: in order to resume a conversation from a KV cache prefix at time `t`, an uncompressed sliding window ending at time `t` would have to be preserved, and a full coverage over resumption points essentially means no compression.

This API does not have support for sliding windows, and therefore has full support for prefix caching.

## Cache Compression API

### Plugin API

HiCache compression codecs are implemented as `HostKVCache` subclasses and selected independently for each KV-cache pool kind, such as MHA, MLA, Mamba, or DSA, and each role such as `lm` or `draft` model.
The design follows a _factory_ pattern, similar to that already used for L3 through `StorageBackendFactory`. A registry maps short codec names to Python classes, implementations are loaded lazily, and external codecs may be loaded dynamically.

Importantly, compression is optional and does not change the current default behavior.

#### Configuration

A single server argument, `--hicache-kvcache-codec`, defines the codec configuration. It accepts either an inline JSON string or an `@file` reference.

The configuration has two levels:

1. **Model role:** `lm` for the target model and `draft` for the MTP or speculative-decoding model.
2. **Pool kind:** `mha`, `mla`, `mamba`, `dsa`, etc.

Each pool maps to a codec specification:

```json
{
  "lm": {
    "mha": {
      "codec": "kvtc"
    },
    "mla": {
      "codec": "kvtc-mla",
      "config": "@/etc/kvtc/mla.json"
    },
    "mamba": {
      "codec": "dynamic",
      "module_path": "acme.codecs",
      "class_name": "AcmeMambaCodec"
    }
  },
  "draft": {
    "mha": {
      "codec": "kvtc"
    }
  }
}
```

 * A specification may reference a registered codec name or use `dynamic` to import an arbitrary module and class. A `dynamic` specification must supply both `module_path` and `class_name`, mirroring the required fields of `StorageBackendFactory._create_dynamic_backend`. The optional `config` field is passed directly to the codec.
 * Omitted roles and pool kinds keep their built-in host pools. For example, omitting `draft` leaves the speculative model unchanged.
 * A codec used for the draft model must validate against the actual draft pool, as the draft model may have different layer counts, head dimensions, layouts, or data types.

#### Registry and loading

The proposed registry mirrors `StorageBackendFactory`:

```python
HostKVCacheFactory.register(
    name,
    module_path,
    class_name,
)
```

`HostKVCacheFactory.resolve()` should:

1. Find the registered module and class, or read them from a `dynamic` specification.
2. Import the module lazily with `importlib`.
3. Retrieve the requested class.
4. Verify that it is a subclass of `HostKVCache`.

Invalid codec names, import failures, and incompatible classes should fail during initialization with an error that identifies the model role and pool kind.

#### Pool construction

All host-pool creation sites should use one shared dispatch helper. The helper receives the device pool, pool kind, model role, server configuration, and pool-specific constructor arguments.

```python
def create_host_kv_pool(
    device_pool,
    kind,
    server_args,
    role="lm",
    **pool_kwargs,
) -> HostKVCache:
    spec = (
        codec_map(server_args.hicache_kvcache_codec)
        .get(role, {})
        .get(kind)
    )

    if spec is None:
        return create_builtin_host_pool(
            device_pool,
            kind,
            **pool_kwargs,
        )

    codec_cls = HostKVCacheFactory.resolve(
        spec["codec"],
        spec,
    )

    return codec_cls(
        device_pool,
        codec_config=spec.get("config"),
        **pool_kwargs,
    )
```

The target-model path passes `role="lm"`, while the draft-model path passes `role="draft"`.

Built-in host pools do not share one constructor signature. For example:

* `MambaPoolHost` does not take `page_size`;
* `DSAIndexerPoolHost` requires an `anchor_host`;
* the MHA implementation may depend on the concrete device-pool type.

Each call site should therefore continue preparing the arguments it already uses and pass them through the shared helper. The helper centralizes codec selection but does not hide pool-specific construction requirements.

A codec is a normal `HostKVCache` subclass. It may inherit from the matching built-in host pool to reuse allocation, indexing, and page I/O, overriding only the compression and decompression behavior.

#### `HostKVCache` interface

Many fixed-rate codecs can already be implemented using the current `HostKVCache` interface in `sglang/srt/mem_cache/pool_host/base.py`:

```python
class HostKVCache(abc.ABC):
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def load_to_device_per_layer(
        self,
        device_pool,
        host_indices,
        device_indices,
        layer_id,
        io_backend,
    ) -> None:
        ...

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def backup_from_device_all_layer(
        self,
        device_pool,
        host_indices,
        device_indices,
        io_backend,
    ) -> None:
        ...

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def get_data_page(
        self,
        index,
        flat: bool = True,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        ...

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def set_from_flat_data_page(
        self,
        index: int,
        data_page: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> None:
        ...
```

A codec can compress data in `backup_from_device_all_layer()` and decompress one layer in `load_to_device_per_layer()`. Page serialization can be implemented through `get_data_page()` and `set_from_flat_data_page()`.

The current interface is missing two capabilities required by some codecs.

First, codecs may need the original sequence positions of the transferred tokens. Host and device slot indices do not necessarily represent sequence positions. Backup and load operations should therefore optionally receive position metadata aligned with the transferred entries.

Second, some codecs compress jointly across layers. The interface currently loads only one layer at a time. It should provide a multi-layer load operation, with a default implementation that repeatedly calls `load_to_device_per_layer()`.

```python
def load_to_device_layers_streaming(
    self,
    device_pool,
    host_indices,
    device_indices,
    layer_ids: Iterable[int],
    io_backend,
    positions: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,  # positions in context (see below)
) -> Iterator[bool]:
    for layer_id in layer_ids:
        self.load_to_device_per_layer(
            device_pool=device_pool,
            host_indices=host_indices,
            device_indices=device_indices,
            layer_id=layer_id,
            io_backend=io_backend,
            positions=positions,
        )
        yield True
```

Codecs with cross-layer dependencies may override this method and decode several layers in one operation.

The factory validates that a plugin is a `HostKVCache` subclass. The codec itself remains responsible for validating compatibility with the concrete pool, including its kind, layout, shape, page size, and data type.


## Changes to the Framework

### 1. Pass Sequence Positions Through Host-Pool Transfers

Some codecs can improve compression by removing position-dependent transformations, such as RoPE, before encoding the KV cache and restoring them after decoding [KVTC, ShadowKV, KVQuant]. To do this, the codec must know the position ID associated with every transferred token.

Host-pool transfer methods should accept an optional `positions` tensor.
There are two cases:

1. **One-dimensional contiguous positions.**
   Standard RoPE models commonly assign positions `0, 1, 2, ...` along the sequence. HiRadix can reconstruct these positions from the location of a node in the radix tree.
   `positions` is a one-dimensional integer tensor with one entry per transferred token.

2. **Non-contiguous or multidimensional positions.**
   Models using schemes such as M-RoPE may associate each token with several position IDs or with positions that cannot be inferred from sequence length. For these models, HiCache must preserve the actual position IDs produced by the model.
   `positions` should allow additional dimensions.

In both cases, position metadata must remain aligned with the transferred host and device indices, and the token dimension aligned with `host_indices` and `device_indices`.


```python
def backup_from_device_all_layer(
    self,
    device_pool,
    host_indices,
    device_indices,
    io_backend,
    positions: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
) -> None:
    ...

def load_to_device_per_layer(
    self,
    device_pool,
    host_indices,
    device_indices,
    layer_id,
    io_backend,
    positions: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
) -> None:
    ...
```

Pools that do not use positions may ignore the argument. Alternatively, the controller may provide it only to pools that advertise a capability such as `wants_positions = True`.

#### One-Dimensional Contiguous Positions

For standard contiguous position IDs, HiRadix can derive the first position represented by a node from its radix-tree depth:

```text
seq_offset(node) = seq_offset(node.parent) + len(node.parent.key)
```

This value can be memoized on the node. When `_split_node` replaces `child` with `new_node -> child`, the cached offsets must be updated:

```python
old_offset = getattr(child, "_seq_offset", None)

new_node._seq_offset = old_offset
child._seq_offset = (
    None if old_offset is None
    else old_offset + split_len
)
```

A contiguous transfer beginning at `node` can then construct:

```python
positions = torch.arange(
    seq_offset(node),
    seq_offset(node) + num_tokens,
    dtype=torch.int64,
)
```

This avoids storing position metadata for every cached token while still providing codecs with the positions needed to reverse and reapply one-dimensional RoPE.

#### Multidimensional and Non-Contiguous Positions (optional)

Radix-tree depth is insufficient for models whose position IDs are multidimensional, discontinuous, or otherwise not determined only by token order.

For these models, HiCache must capture the actual position IDs used during model execution and attach them to the corresponding cache entries. The precise tensor shape depends on the model's positional scheme, but one dimension must correspond to the transferred tokens.

These positions must be stored or reconstructed together with the cache metadata. They cannot be replaced by a simple `torch.arange` without changing the meaning of the cached keys.

Alternatively, implementation of this feature might be postponed, and left unsupported for codecs which require those positions.

#### Operation Propagation

Operation propagation is required for both cases. Even when one-dimensional positions are reconstructed by HiRadix, the resulting tensor must still travel with the cache operation from the radix-tree layer to the host pool.

`CacheOperation` should therefore carry position metadata through the write and load queues:

```python
class CacheOperation:
    def __init__(
        self,
        host_indices: torch.Tensor,
        device_indices: torch.Tensor,
        node_id: int,
        priority: Optional[int] = None,
        positions: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
    ):
        self.host_indices = host_indices
        self.device_indices = device_indices
        self.positions = positions
        ...
```

Merged operations must either all contain position metadata or all omit it:

```python
has_positions = [op.positions is not None for op in ops]

if any(has_positions) and not all(has_positions):
    raise ValueError(
        "Cannot merge operations with mixed position metadata"
    )

merged_op.positions = (
    torch.cat([op.positions for op in ops], dim=-1)
    if all(has_positions)
    else None
)
```

The concatenation dimension should be the token dimension. For one-dimensional positions this is the only dimension; for multidimensional positions it must be defined explicitly by the position-tensor contract.

Every transformation applied to cache indices must also be applied to positions. For example, if the `direct` backend sorts `host_indices`, the same permutation must reorder `device_indices` and the token dimension of `positions`. Otherwise, the codec receives valid position IDs associated with the wrong tokens.

This applies in particular to `move_indices` in `sglang/srt/managers/cache_controller.py`.

The current codebase contains two controller-level operation classes:

* `sglang/srt/managers/cache_controller.py::CacheOperation`
* `sglang/srt/mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_cache_controller.py::CacheOperation`

Both classes, their `merge_ops` implementations, and their `write`, `load`, `start_writing`, and `start_loading` paths must preserve position metadata.


#### 2. Support codecs that operate on layer groups

The current load path calls `load_to_device_per_layer` once per layer. This works for a per-layer codec, but it is inefficient for codecs whose transform jointly encodes several layers [X, Y]. Such a codec may otherwise decode the same layer group repeatedly or stage the entire decoded result behind the per-layer API.

There is already one precedent for a grouped transfer hidden behind this API: with `io_backend="kernel_ascend"` and the `page_first_direct` layout, `MHATokenToKVPoolHost.load_to_device_per_layer` transfers all layers when `layer_id == 0` and is a no-op for every other layer id. A grouped-load API must keep that pattern expressible.

We propose a new generator-based method that yields once per layer, as soon as the transfer for that layer has been enqueued. The controller remains responsible for assigning the local layer index and recording the corresponding completion event:

```python
def load_to_device_layers_streaming(
    self,
    device_pool,
    host_indices,
    device_indices,
    layer_ids: Iterable[int],
    io_backend,
    positions: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
) -> Iterator[bool]:
    for layer_id in layer_ids:
        self.load_to_device_per_layer(
            device_pool=device_pool,
            host_indices=host_indices,
            device_indices=device_indices,
            layer_id=layer_id,
            io_backend=io_backend,
            positions=positions,
        )
        yield True
```

The corresponding controller change follows the structure of the existing `start_loading` loop in the base `HiCacheController`:

```python
_EXHAUSTED = object()

layer_loading = self.mem_pool_host.load_to_device_layers_streaming(
    self.mem_pool_device,
    host_indices,
    device_indices,
    range(self.layer_num),
    self.io_backend,
    positions=op.positions,
)

draft_layer_loading = None
draft_layer_num = 0
# Hoisted out of the loop from the existing per-layer
# `i < self.mem_pool_host_draft.layer_num` check.
if self.has_draft:
    draft_layer_num = min(self.layer_num, self.mem_pool_host_draft.layer_num)
    draft_layer_loading = self.mem_pool_host_draft.load_to_device_layers_streaming(
        self.mem_pool_device_draft,
        host_indices,
        device_indices,
        range(draft_layer_num),
        self.io_backend,
        positions=op.positions,
    )

for i, _ in zip(range(self.layer_num), layer_loading, strict=True):
    if draft_layer_loading is not None and i < draft_layer_num:
        if next(draft_layer_loading, _EXHAUSTED) is _EXHAUSTED:
            raise ValueError("Draft layer loader yielded too few layers")
    producer_event.complete(i)

if (
    draft_layer_loading is not None
    and next(draft_layer_loading, _EXHAUSTED) is not _EXHAUSTED
):
    raise ValueError("Draft layer loader yielded too many layers")
```

The generator must yield exactly once for every element of `layer_ids`, in the same order. `zip(..., strict=True)` enforces this cardinality for the target pool. The draft iterator is shorter, so it is driven manually: the `_EXHAUSTED` default of `next()` reports early exhaustion instead of raising `StopIteration` inside the loop, and the final `next()` detects surplus yields. The yielded value itself is not inspected, because the default implementation yields `True`. The completion event is therefore recorded only after both the target and, when present, draft KV caches for that layer have been enqueued.

This default implementation preserves existing behavior. A grouped codec may decode multiple layers in one operation and then yield once for each layer that the operation covers. The per-layer yields preserve the current synchronization contract and allow model execution to overlap with loading later layer groups.

An all-layers fast path is a valid specialization, but it gives up the existing load/compute overlap if it does not yield until every layer has been enqueued.

Both current implementations of `start_loading` must be changed: the base `HiCacheController` and `HybridCacheController`. The two do not guard the draft transfer identically. The base controller only checks `i < self.mem_pool_host_draft.layer_num`, while `HybridCacheController` additionally requires `host_indices.numel() > 0`, because its `load()` can enqueue an operation with no KV tokens. That extra condition must be preserved when the draft loader is hoisted out of the loop, otherwise an empty transfer would reach the draft pool. `HostPoolGroup` also needs the
analogous streaming forwarding implementation, preserving its `pool_transfers` argument alongside `positions`. The
`_preload_to_device_buffer` and `naive_load_topk` methods in `hisparse_coordinator.py` are separate per-layer call sites. The latter is a debugging and unit-test oracle, while production uses `swap_in_selected_pages`. These paths can remain per-layer unless grouped-codec support is required for HiSparse.

### 3. Provide codec construction context explicitly

A codec may need TP or PP ranks and cache metadata to select and validate rank-specific parameters. The framework should provide this context without adding many loosely related arguments to every `HostKVCache` constructor.

The initial integration requires the following changes:

* Add a `codec_config` argument when constructing a codec-backed host pool. The value may be an inline JSON object or a path to a JSON file.
* Pass the active `device_pool` to the codec, as existing host-pool constructors already do.
* Ensure that `device_pool` exposes the metadata needed by the codec, including cache shape, dtype, local layer range, and the local head or state fragments owned by the current rank.

The codec can obtain the current TP and PP ranks through SGLang's existing distributed helpers:

```python
get_tensor_model_parallel_rank()
get_pipeline_model_parallel_rank()
```

The `HostKVCache` base interface does not require a substantial redesign. The main framework change is in the codec construction path: it must pass `codec_config` and provide a `device_pool` that exposes all required local cache metadata. If some ownership information is not currently available from `device_pool`, that metadata must be added explicitly.

### 4. Track Compression State Across L1–L2 and L2–L3

Compression may be applied at either transfer boundary:

```text
L1 device cache <-> L2 host cache <-> L3 storage
                 ^                 ^
              L1-L2 codec       L2-L3 codec
```

Both codecs may use heuristics. For example, a codec may compress only sufficiently long sequences, selected pool kinds, pages for which compression is expected to be beneficial. Configuration therefore defines **when a codec may compress**, but HiCache must record the actual decision separately for every page. In particular, no page should be compressed twice.

**Transfer Behavior**  

On an L1-to-L2 transfer, the L1–L2 codec decides whether to compress the page. HiCache stores either the encoded representation or the original host representation and records the resulting state.

On an L2-to-L3 transfer:

* If the page is `uncompressed`, the L2–L3 codec may compress it according to its own policy.
* If the page is already compressed, it is transferred to L3 verbatim as an opaque blob.
* If the L2–L3 codec declines to compress an uncompressed page, the original L2 page is stored verbatim.

The reverse path follows the policy configured in the codec: a compressed object might be decoded either during L3-to-L2 transfer or L2-to-L1 transfer.

**Compression Metadata**  

Compression state must be tracked per page, not only per host pool or request, because heuristic decisions may differ between pages in the same cache.

Each L3 object must preserve enough metadata to determine how it should be restored. At minimum, this includes:
* whether the page is compressed;
* the codec identifier and format version.

The framework must not infer compression state from payload size or configuration. A codec may be configured but choose not to compress a particular page.

This metadata may be stored in a small object header or passed through an explicit page descriptor. If `get_data_page()` and `set_from_flat_data_page()` continue to exchange only tensors, the returned blob must be self-describing. Otherwise, these methods must be extended to pass the compression descriptor together with the payload.

State changes must become visible only after the corresponding asynchronous encode, transfer, and write operation has completed successfully.

**Whole-Page L3 Semantics**  

The initial L2–L3 API should preserve the existing whole-page behavior. `_generic_page_set` reads one complete L2 page through `get_data_page()`, and `_generic_page_get` restores one complete page through `set_from_flat_data_page()`.

An encoded page is therefore one opaque L3 object and must be decodable as a complete unit. Sub-page reads and writes are not supported. Codecs that require several pages or layer groups as one encoding unit need a separate grouped-I/O interface.

Head splitting is supported only when the active representation can be divided into independently decodable head shards. A codec that mixes information across heads must declare head splitting unsupported and reject `should_split_heads` during initialization. An uncompressed page may continue to use the existing head-splitting path.

Position metadata is required only when the codec that actually performs the encoding uses it. For example, an L2–L3 codec that removes RoPE from an otherwise uncompressed page must receive the relevant positions (store them along with cache during L1–L2 call). A page already compressed on the L1–L2 path is transferred to L3 opaquely and does not require positions again.

Unsupported combinations—such as nested compression, missing position metadata, incompatible head splitting, or an L3 backend that cannot store the codec’s output format—must fail explicitly rather than silently falling back to an incorrect representation.

### 5. Variable-size blob storage (optional)

Fixed-rate codecs can continue to use the existing slot allocator because each compressed page has a fixed encoded size. Variable-rate codecs, especially entropy coders, need a blob allocator to realize their memory savings at L2. Reserving every slot at the worst-case compressed size is correct but largely defeats variable-rate compression.

A reusable blob manager should allocate variable-size byte ranges and track at least the blob offset, encoded length, codec/configuration identifier, and enough metadata to validate and decode the blob. It should also define compaction, fragmentation, lifetime, and concurrency behavior. This manager is not required for KVTC, but it would prevent each future variable-rate codec from reimplementing host-storage mechanics.

items.title: [Bug] Qwen3.5 greedy outputs differ A LOT between v0.5.12 and v0.5.17.dev for the same multimodal request; v0.5.17.dev36 not self-consistent behind router
items.body:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are included below.

## Describe the bug

We serve the same VLM (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) with two SGLang builds on identical
hardware (NVIDIA H20, TP=1, 4 independent workers behind the SGLang router):

- Build A: **v0.5.12** (commit `5a15cde858ea09b77`)
- Build B: **v0.5.17.dev36+gcb05a44** (commit `cb05a44`)

Sending a **byte-identical** multimodal request (`prompt_tokens` = 3932 on both
builds) with `temperature=0`:

### 1. A and B produce substantially different outputs

The fork always happens in the same region — right after the shared prefix
`"... This is exactly what I need(ed)"` (output char ~149–162) — and the
continuations then diverge completely:

| | completion tokens | stable across repeats? |
|---|---|---|
| A (0.5.12) | 246 | yes, bit-stable |
| B (0.5.17.dev36) | 342/342/342 in one session; 282/134/134 in a later session | **no** |

Cross-build text similarity: 0.28–0.58.

### 2. B is not self-consistent at temperature=0

Across repeated identical requests behind the router, B returned 342/342/342
completion tokens in one session but 282/134/134 in a later one (see
`results/repro_verify.log` in the attachment). A is bit-stable across all
repeats. The router round-robins over 4 identical workers, so this points at
worker-level non-determinism at temperature=0 on v0.5.17.dev.

### 3. The divergence is an argmax flip on a near-tie

With `logprobs=True`, at the first divergence position (right after
`"... This is exactly what I "`):

| Build | top-1 | top-2 | top-2 logprob gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5.12 | `need` (-0.7474) | `needed` (-0.7474) | **0.0** |
| 0.5.17.dev36 | `needed` (-0.6269) | `need` (-0.8769) | 0.25 |

Each build picks a different winner and the free-form `<think>` continuation
diverges completely. In a later session the flip lands one token later
(`' accomplish'` with gap 0.625 on A vs `' see'` with gap 0.125 on B).
`prompt_tokens` is identical (3932) on both builds, so tokenization / image
preprocessing are not the cause.

### Real-world impact: the flip changes grounded-action coordinates

We first hit this while serving an SFT checkpoint of the same model in a
GUI-agent (computer-use) setting. The model outputs `left_click` actions with
screen coordinates; at one step of a task ("remove vim from the favorites
bar"), the identical request produced **semantically different actions** on the
two builds:

| Build | model coordinate (normalized) | scaled click @1920x1080 | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5.12 | `[87, 95]` | (167, 102) — center of the "Remove from Favorites" context-menu item | menu item clicked → **task succeeds** |
| 0.5.17.dev36 | `[217, 91]` / `[164, 91]` (varies across repeats) | (417, 98) / (315, 98) — ~250px away, misses the menu entirely | clicks a wrong element → **task fails** |

The reference trajectory from which this request was replayed succeeded with
exactly 0.5.12's action. Across 8 repeated identical requests, v0.5.17.dev36
**never** produced the correct coordinate: the argmax flip landed on the
leading digit of the x-coordinate, and autoregressive conditioning then kept
the rest of the number consistently wrong.

So the divergence is not limited to free-form `<think>` text: when the flipped
token is part of a grounded action (a coordinate), it changes which UI element
gets clicked and flips task success/failure — which makes cross-build
evaluation results non-comparable for agent workloads.

## Reproduction

Repro package: **`sglang_issue_repro.zip`** (attached below)

[sglang_issue_repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31462585/sglang_issue_repro.zip)

Contents:

- `request_step1.json` — the exact request payload (OpenAI
  `/v1/chat/completions` format: system + 1 history turn + current turn, 2
  base64 PNG screenshots, `temperature=0, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=2048`,
  `enable_thinking=True`)
- `repro_compare.py` — standalone repro script (only needs `openai>=1.x`);
  sends the request N times to each endpoint and reports self-consistency,
  cross-version similarity, first divergence position, and (with `--logprobs`)
  the top-2 logprob gap at the diverging token
- `results/observed_outputs.json` — captured outputs of the first experiment
  (3 repeats per build + per-token top-2 logprobs around the divergence)
- `results/repro_verify.log` — a later verification run (3 repeats per build)
  showing v0.5.17.dev failing self-consistency behind the router
- `server_args/` — verbatim `ServerArgs(...)` from a worker log of each build
  (host / model path scrubbed)

```bash
pip install openai
python repro_compare.py \
    --request request_step1.json \
    --endpoint-a http://<server-a>:30000/v1 \
    --endpoint-b http://<server-b>:30000/v1 \
    --label-a sglang-0.5.12 --label-b sglang-0.5.17.dev36 \
    --runs 3 --logprobs
```

Expected: identical `prompt_tokens` on both builds; outputs differ; first
divergence right after `"... This is exactly what I need(ed)"` with a top-2
logprob gap ≤ 0.25 at the diverging token.

## Environment

- SGLang builds: `0.5.12` (commit `5a15cde858ea09b77`) vs
  `0.5.17.dev36+gcb05a44` (commit `cb05a44`)
- Model: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (VL), bfloat16, `context_length=32768`
- Hardware: NVIDIA H20, one worker per GPU, 4 workers behind the SGLang router
- Both builds launched with the same effective core arguments:
  `attention_backend='fa3'`, `sampling_backend='flashinfer'`,
  `mem_fraction_static=0.9`, `max_running_requests=16`,
  `chunked_prefill_size=8192`, `schedule_policy='fcfs'`, `page_size=1`,
  TP=1, radix cache enabled, cuda graphs enabled
- Full `ServerArgs` for both builds: `server_args/` in the attachment

Differences in effective `ServerArgs` between the two builds (all other keys
identical):

| key | 0.5.12 | 0.5.17.dev36 | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `disable_overlap_schedule` | `True` (auto-forced: *"Disabling overlap schedule since mamba no_buffer is not compatible with overlap schedule"*) | `False` | 0.5.17 switches `mamba_radix_cache_strategy` from `no_buffer` to `extra_buffer`, which re-enables the overlap scheduler |
| cuda graph config | decode-only graphs (`cuda_graph_max_bs=256`, `disable_piecewise_cuda_graph=True`) | `cuda_graph_config` with **prefill breakable cuda graph** enabled (`tc_compiler='eager'`) | prefill also runs inside captured graphs on 0.5.17.dev |

### Questions

1. Is cross-build numeric divergence of greedy (temperature=0) outputs expected
   given the scheduler / cuda-graph changes above?
2. For v0.5.17.dev, is the router-level non-self-consistency (different workers
   → different greedy outputs for the same request) a known limitation? Is
   there a recommended configuration to make each worker — and workers
   mutually — bit-stable (e.g. disabling prefill cuda graphs / the overlap
   scheduler, or `enable_deterministic_inference`)?

items.title: [Perf] NEXTN/EAGLE: draft embed_tokens/lm_head copies are released after KV pool sizing, significantly shrinking max_total_num_tokens
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version (verified on `main` as of 2026-08-26).
- [x] This is a performance/resource-efficiency issue with a clear root cause and a tested workaround.

### Describe the bug

When running speculative decoding (`--speculative-algorithm NEXTN`, which resolves to
the EAGLE algorithm and `EAGLEWorkerV2`), the draft model allocates its own
`embed_tokens.weight` and `lm_head.weight` during construction:

- `VocabParallelEmbedding` for `embed_tokens` is built **without** `quant_config`
  → always bf16.
- `ParallelLMHead` receives the fp8 `quant_config`, but
  `Fp8Config.get_quant_method()` returns `None` for embedding-type layers → falls back
  to `UnquantizedEmbeddingMethod` → also bf16.

For a model with `vocab_size=248320, hidden_size=5120`, each tensor is **2.54 GiB**,
i.e. **~5.08 GiB total**. These two tensors are **never loaded from the checkpoint**
(`mtp.*` keys contain no embed/lm_head) — they hold random-init garbage whose only
fate is to be `del`'d in `set_embed_and_head()`, which rebinds them to the target
model's weights.

The problem is **when** that release happens. The call chain is:

```
scheduler init:
  init_tp_model_worker()          # target weights
  maybe_init_draft_worker()       # draft weights (stale copies now occupy ~5 GiB)
  init_memory_pools():
    target ModelRunner.alloc_memory_pool()
      └─ KVCacheConfigurator.configure()
           └─ get_available_gpu_memory()     # ★ KV pool budget measured HERE,
                                             #   while the 5 GiB stale copies still count as used
    EAGLEWorkerV2.alloc_memory_pool()
      ├─ draft_worker.alloc_memory_pool()
      ├─ init_token_map()
      └─ init_lm_head()                       # ★ del + rebind + torch.cuda.empty_cache()
                                              #   happen HERE — too late for KV sizing
```

So the KV pool is sized with ~5 GiB less free VRAM than actually available, and the
subsequent release cannot retroactively grow `max_total_num_tokens`.

**Verified on `main` (2026-08-26):** the class was refactored into
`EagleDraftWorker` nested in `EAGLEWorkerV2`, but the ordering is unchanged —
`init_token_map()` / `init_lm_head()` are still called at the tail of
`alloc_memory_pool()`, after the target KV pool sizing read.

### Measured impact (single GPU, 1× RTX 4090 48GB, TP=PP=DP=1, `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18`)

Model: Qwen3.5-27B-class FP8 hybrid (GDN) multimodal model,
`--speculative-algorithm NEXTN --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1
--speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 --max-running-requests 4 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 4
--max-mamba-cache-size 24`.

| Metric | Stock v0.5.18 | With timing patch |
|---|---|---|
| draft weight load footprint | 5.19 GB | 5.19 GB |
| avail mem right after KV pool sizing | 4.08 GB | 3.82 GB |
| avail mem bump before CUDA-graph capture ("late release") | +4.19 GB (4.08 → 8.27) | **none** (already released pre-sizing) |
| **`max_total_num_tokens`** | **149,806** | **305,070 (+103.7%)** |

The freed ~5 GiB went entirely into the KV pool where it belongs. Speculative
decoding itself is unaffected (accept length ~2.8, accept rate ~0.6, unchanged),
and an 8-way concurrency stress test (4 running + 4 queued, incl. an 8k-token
prompt) passed with zero errors.

### Proposed fix

Move `init_token_map()` + `init_lm_head()` from the tail of `alloc_memory_pool()`
to the end of the worker's `__init__` (right after `self.draft_runner` is
assigned). All three dependencies of `init_lm_head()` are ready at that point —
target model (loaded), `draft_runner.model` (loaded), `hot_token_id` (only reads
spec args / the token-map file) — and none of them touches any memory pool.

Keep a guarded fallback in `alloc_memory_pool()` for the unit-test harnesses that
skip `__init__` (they already rely on this pattern for
`_init_dsa_index_share_state`):

```python
# in __init__, after self.draft_runner = self.draft_worker.model_runner
self.init_token_map()
self.init_lm_head()
self._lm_head_shared = True

# in alloc_memory_pool(), replacing the unconditional calls
if not getattr(self, "_lm_head_shared", False):
    self.init_token_map()
    self.init_lm_head()
```

I have this running in production as a local patch (anchor-checked, revertible);
happy to open a PR if the approach looks right.

### Environment

- SGLang: `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18` (also verified on `main` source)
- GPU: 1× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 48GB (49140 MiB); TP=1, PP=1, DP=1 — no tensor/pipeline parallelism involved
- Model: FP8 (w8a8 block) hybrid GDN + full-attention, vocab 248320, hidden 5120,
  `tie_word_embeddings=False`
- Speculative: NEXTN 3/1/4

### Acknowledgements / how this report was made

This issue originates from me, while comparing SGLang vs vLLM startup memory
footprints for the same model under identical settings, noticed SGLang's KV pool was
significantly smaller, identified draft-head weight sharing as the likely cause, and
set the direction. The root-cause analysis, patch development, and validation were
then carried out by an AI coding assistant (Kimi, Moonshot AI) working against the
official documentation and open-source community discussions, with me reviewing
and testing every step end to end. Credit for the findings is shared between the
 the AI, and the community work below:

References consulted:

- vLLM MTP speculative decoding docs — the reference behavior that revealed the gap:
  https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/features/speculative_decoding/mtp.md
- SGLang weight-loader RFC (`load_weights` / tie-word-embeddings boilerplate): #24703
- MTP `get_embed_and_head` interface gaps on other model families: #31236
- Qwen3.5 MTP community practice: #23123
````

items.title: [Bug][NPU] ModelSlim W8A8 checkpoint of Qwen3.8-27B (GDN hybrid) loads with garbage weights: fused in_proj_qkvz scheme unresolved, vision encoder forced unquantized; NPU quant matmul crashes on 3-D vision input
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

  Environment

  - SGLang version: release/v0.5.18 (with Ascend NPU backports)
  - Hardware: Ascend NPU, CANN 9.0.0 / torch_npu; container quay.io/ascend/sglang:v0.5.18-cann9.0.0-a3
  - Model: Qwen3.8-27B-w8a8 — ModelSlim W8A8_DYNAMIC export of Qwen3.5-27B (48 GatedDeltaNet linear-attention layers with fused in_proj_qkvz/in_proj_ba, 16 full-attention layers, vision tower)

  Reproduction

  sglang serve --model-path /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-w8a8/ \
      --quantization modelslim --device npu --tp-size 2

  The checkpoint is a proper ModelSlim export: quant_model_description.json marks the fused-GDN shards and the vision tower as W8A8_DYNAMIC, and the weight index contains all 440 weight_scale/weight_offset pairs.

  Actual behavior (three independent failures)

  1. Fused GDN layers silently fall back to unquantized — 48 warnings, then the checkpoint's int8 weights are copied raw into bf16 params (no error, garbage model output):

  Unsupported Linear modelslim scheme: [''] in layer: model.language_model.layers.N.linear_attn.in_proj_qkvz   (all 48 GDN layers)
  Parameter model.layers.N.linear_attn.in_proj_qkvz.weight_scale / weight_offset not found in params_dict

  2. Vision encoder forced unquantized — 162 warnings (27 blocks × attn.qkv_proj / attn.proj / mlp.linear_fc1 × 2 params):

  Parameter visual.blocks.N.attn.qkv_proj.weight_scale / weight_offset not found in params_dict

  3. With 1 and 2 fixed, the server crashes at warmup in the first quantized vision matmul:

  RuntimeError: npu_quant_matmul: ... QuantMatmulKernelNpuOpApi.cpp:297 NPU function error: call aclnnQuantMatmulV5 failed, error code is 161002
  AclNN_Parameter_Error(EZ1001): When x1Scale(pertokenScale), x2Scale(scale) both have only one dimension, the shape of x1Scale(pertokenScale) should be (1) or (m), m represents the size of m dimension of x1, which is 1. Actual
  shape of x1Scale(pertokenScale): (256).

  Root causes

  1. layers/quantization/modelslim/modelslim.py — _quant_prefix_candidates() already resolves checkpoint-name layout variants (mlp ↔ block_sparse_moe, outer language_model prefix), but not the Qwen3.5-GDN fused projections: the
     model side fuses in_proj_qkv + in_proj_z → in_proj_qkvz (and in_proj_b + in_proj_a → in_proj_ba) while the checkpoint keeps the unfused per-projection names. Scheme lookup misses → get_linear_scheme() returns None →
     UnquantizedLinearMethod() → weight_scale/weight_offset params never created, int8 weight loads raw into the bf16 param.
  2. models/qwen3_vl.py — Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration.__init__ hardcodes quant_config=None for Qwen3VLMoeVisionModel (the comment only considers BitsAndBytes/GPTQ/AWQ). ModelSlim checkpoints quantize the vision tower
     (attn.qkv/attn.proj/mlp.linear_fc1 are W8A8_DYNAMIC), so those weights load as garbage too.
  3. hardware_backend/npu/quantization/linear_method_npu.py — NPUW8A8Int8LinearMethod/NPUW8A8Int8DynamicLinearMethod.apply pass x straight to npu_dynamic_quant/npu_quantize/npu_quant_matmul. The vision tower always feeds
     linears 3-D (seq, 1, hidden) activations (x.unsqueeze(1) in Qwen3VLMoeVisionModel.forward), and the NPU quant ops only accept 2-D. The bf16 path broadcasts 3-D fine, which is why this only appears once the vision tower is
     quantized.

## Describe the bug

DeepSeek-V4-Flash (block-FP8) on 8x MI300X (gfx942), TP8, produces **correct output at short context and progressively degraded output as prompt length grows**. It never crashes, never NaNs, and emits no error — the text simply decays.

Length sweep, single node, greedy (`temperature=0`), same trailing question with increasing neutral filler prepended:

| prompt length | continuation | verdict |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| ~13 tok | `" blue and the grass is green"` | correct |
| ~103 tok | `". The sky is blue"` | correct |
| ~303 tok | `".. A."` | broken |
| ~603 tok | `"..."` | broken |
| ~1503 tok | `"\n.84."` | broken |

Factual probe (prompt ends `"... Rome is the capital of"`, expected `" Italy"`):

| ~130 | ~230 | ~250 | ~270 | ~290 | ~310 | ~330 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ` Italy` | ` Italy` | ` Italy` | ` Italy` | ` Italy` | ` France` | ` Italy` |

Note this is **not a hard cliff at a page/window boundary** — `" Italy"` appears and disappears across 230–330 tokens. The degradation is smooth and probabilistic with length, which looks like a compounding numerical error rather than a discrete indexing bug.

Needle-in-a-haystack: **0/3 hits at every length tested**, including 3k. Above ~2048 tokens the output is additionally **non-deterministic** across identical greedy requests; below that it is deterministic-but-wrong.

## What we have already ruled out

We replaced each DSA component with an alternate or reference implementation. **Every one of these produces byte-identical wrong output** (`cont@1500 == "\n.84."`):

| swap | how | cont@1500 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baseline | — | `\n.84.` |
| whole compressor implementation | `SGLANG_OPT_USE_OLD_COMPRESSOR=1` | `\n.84.` |
| non-paged indexer | non-paged path | `\n.84.` |
| **core MLA attention** | tilelang sparse attention backend | `\n.84.` |
| CUDA-path norm + old compressor | JIT norm + old compress | `\n.84.` |
| **indexer scoring + top-k, both pure torch** | torch logits + torch topk | `\n.84.` |

So the defect does **not** appear to be in the compressor, indexer scoring, top-k selection, MoE runner, or the sparse attention kernel — swapping the entire sparse stack changes nothing at all.

FP8 GEMM backend sweep (~15 configurations). Only **one** flag ever changed the output:

| config | cont@1500 |
| --- | --- |
| `--fp8-gemm-backend triton` | `\n.84.` (unchanged) |
| `--fp8-gemm-backend cutlass` | `\n.84.` (unchanged) |
| `--fp8-gemm-backend deep_gemm` | `\n.84.` (unchanged) |
| `SGLANG_USE_AITER_FP8_PER_TOKEN=1` | `\n.84.` (unchanged) |
| `SGLANG_OPT_FP8_WO_A_GEMM=0` | `\n.84.` (unchanged) |
| **`USE_TRITON_W8A8_FP8_KERNEL=1`** | **`\n.84c8` ← changed** |

`USE_TRITON_W8A8_FP8_KERNEL` routes the per-token FP8 matmul (`fp8_utils.py`, the `use_triton_w8a8_fp8_kernel` branch) to `triton_scaled_mm`. It is the only lever that moved the output, which suggests the FP8 linear path is on the causal path — but it changed to a *different* wrong answer, not a correct one.

## Per-layer residual probe

We instrumented `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer.forward` to log the hidden state entering each of the 43 decoder layers (L2 norm, max-abs, NaN/Inf counts), for a short (correct) and a long (broken) prompt:

```
          SHORT (correct)          LONG (broken)
layer  0  norm   11.4  max  0.31   norm   94.6  max  2.38
layer 21  norm  143    max 20.1    norm  196    max 11.3
layer 42  norm  881    max 42.3    norm  412    max 37.3

nan=0  inf=0  on EVERY layer, in BOTH runs
```

No NaN, no Inf, and **no layer where the norm explodes**. Magnitudes stay bounded and grow smoothly in both cases. Whatever is wrong corrupts the *direction* of the residual stream rather than its magnitude — which resembles the compounding per-layer cosine decay reported in #28685 (0.96 → 0.10) more than a single blown-up kernel.

Caveat on this measurement: the short and long prompts differ in content as well as length, so this is indicative rather than a controlled A/B.

## Main question

`python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/fp8_utils.py` contains:

```python
# Force CK bpreshuffle (not Triton) for the dense w8a8-block GEMMs (MLA q/kv/o
# projections), to match ATOM (CK preshuffle; Triton FP8 blockscale is slower).
# Default OFF; DeepseekV4 enables it via set_force_ck_w8a8(True).
_FORCE_CK_W8A8: bool = False
```

**Is the forced CK w8a8 path accuracy-validated on gfx942 for DeepSeek-V4?**

Why we ask:

- On gfx942, `_use_aiter_bpreshuffle_gfx95` is False, so `aiter_w8a8_block_fp8_linear` would normally fall to `else: use_triton = True` — as described in #32516.
- DSV4 specifically calls `set_force_ck_w8a8(True)`, overriding that for the MLA q/kv/o projections, which is exactly the per-layer path carrying the activations.
- #32516 measured Triton↔CK as *quality-neutral* on GLM (PPL 2.850 → 2.912), so the block-GEMM kernel choice alone should not explain this — but that was GLM, not DSV4/DSA.
- #28685 found an aiter blockscale GEMM numerically wrong on gfx950 with a very similar compounding-error signature, and the resolution was to stop using the affected kernel.

Secondary question: **is DSV4-Flash-FP8 on gfx942 expected to be correct at long context today**, or is it still in bring-up? Roadmap #31783 §7 lists DSV4-Flash-FP8 issues (#32553) as open blockers and the ROCm quantization section has many incomplete items, so it is entirely possible we are simply ahead of current support. A clear "not supported yet" answer would be just as useful to us as a fix.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Launch DeepSeek-V4-Flash block-FP8 on a single 8x MI300X node:

```bash
export SGLANG_OPT_SWIGLU_CLAMP_FUSION=0   # required on HIP, see note 2 below
export SGLANG_USE_AITER=1

python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8> \
  --tp-size 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --attention-backend aiter \
  --dsa-prefill-backend aiter \
  --dsa-decode-backend aiter \
  --disable-radix-cache \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \
  --disable-cuda-graph \
  --moe-runner-backend triton \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000
```

2. Send the same factual question with increasing amounts of neutral filler prepended, greedy decoding:

```bash
FILLER="The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. "
for N in 2 20 60 100; do
  P="$(python3 -c "print('$FILLER'*$N, end='')")Rome is the capital of"
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/completions \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"model\":\"<model>\",\"prompt\":$(python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.dumps(sys.argv[1]))" "$P"),\"max_tokens\":8,\"temperature\":0}" \
    | python3 -c "import json,sys;print('N=$N ->', repr(json.load(sys.stdin)['choices'][0]['text']))"
done
```

3. Observe that the completion is `" Italy"` (correct) at short context and degrades to unrelated tokens / punctuation as the filler grows.

## Other ROCm findings from this bring-up

These are separate from the correctness bug above; happy to split them into their own issues or send PRs if useful.

1. **`topk_impl.cuh` does not compile on gfx942.** `jit_kernel/include/sgl_kernel/deepseek_v4/topk_impl.cuh`'s `TopKCluster` specialization uses Hopper distributed shared memory (`cooperative_groups`, `cluster.map_shared_rank`), which has no gfx942 equivalent. `TopKRadixBase`, `TopKRegister`, and `TopKStreaming` are portable. Guarding **only** `TopKCluster` (and the `cooperative_groups` include/alias) behind `#ifndef __HIP_PLATFORM_AMD__` makes `--dsa-topk-backend sgl-kernel` build and run on gfx942. I can send a PR for this.

2. **Several CUDA-only paths are reachable from HIP defaults.** `SGLANG_OPT_SWIGLU_CLAMP_FUSION` defaults to True but dispatches a CUDA-only kernel, so it must be set to 0 on HIP for DSV4 to run. Similarly `SGLANG_OPT_USE_FUSED_CLAMP_ACT_MUL=0` requires `cuda_fp8.h`, and `--fp8-gemm-backend triton` raises an AssertionError on this path.

3. **aiter fused MoE is non-deterministic on gfx942** — identical greedy requests return different logprobs. `--moe-runner-backend triton` restores determinism. This is independent of the correctness bug: the MoE runner choice does not change the wrong output above.

## Environment

- Hardware: 8x AMD Instinct MI300X (gfx942), single node, TP8
- ROCm: 7.2.0
- PyTorch: 2.9.1+rocm7.2.0.git7e1940d4
- SGLang: commit `4ad418d2c3`
- aiter: commit `9127c94a1`
- Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, block-FP8 (128x128 block scales)
- Container: internal image based on the ROCm SGLang build

Happy to run any additional instrumentation or A/B on this hardware — we have a standing multi-node MI300X allocation and can turn experiments around quickly.

items.title: --enable-deterministic-inference accepted and reported enabled, but has no effect on an NVFP4 W4A4 + hybrid-Mamba checkpoint with a DFlash2 drafter (GB10 / sm_121)
items.body:
## Summary

On a GB10 (sm_121, aarch64), `--enable-deterministic-inference` **works
correctly on a dense BF16 model** in the same container image, on the same GPU:
identical concurrent requests collapse from 8 distinct completions to 1.

On a **Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (W4A4) checkpoint with hybrid Mamba layers and a DFlash2
drafter**, the same flag is accepted, appears as
`enable_deterministic_inference=True` in the resolved `ServerArgs`, and
**temperature-0 outputs remain non-reproducible**.

The flag therefore appears not to cover one or more of those paths, and it fails
**silently** — the server reports the feature as on. A user reading the resolved
args has no way to know the guarantee does not apply to their model.

## Why this is worth a report even though the flag "works"

The failure mode is not "deterministic mode is broken". It is **a coverage gap
that presents identically to success**. That is worse than an error, because the
natural check — confirm the flag was applied — passes.

We spent a substantial amount of time excluding four other explanations before
testing the flag against a model simple enough to isolate the hardware. Anyone
running a quantized or hybrid model on this hardware will hit the same wall, and
the resolved-args check will reassure them at exactly the wrong moment.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GB10, sm_121, aarch64 |
| SGLang | `0.0.0.dev1+g5f55db35e` (locally built dev image, commit `5f55db35e`) |
| torch / CUDA | `2.13.0+cu130` / CUDA 13.0 |
| Attention backend | `flashinfer` |
| Working model | Qwen3-0.6B, **dense BF16** |
| Failing model | Qwen3.8-27B **NVFP4 (W4A4)**, hybrid Mamba layers, DFlash2 drafter |

## Reproducer

The probe fires N identical requests concurrently and counts **distinct
completions**. A batch-invariant server returns exactly one.

```python
# batch_invariance_probe.py <base_url> <model> <n>
import collections, concurrent.futures, hashlib, sys, httpx

BASE, MODEL, N = sys.argv[1].rstrip("/"), sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
PROMPT = ("A backup job writes 47 GB on Monday, then 12% more each day for the "
          "next four days. Compute the total written across all five days, "
          "showing each day's figure to two decimal places.")

def one(_):
    r = httpx.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions", timeout=900, json={
        "model": MODEL, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}],
        "max_tokens": 512, "temperature": 0.0})
    r.raise_for_status()
    m = r.json()["choices"][0]["message"]
    text = (m.get("reasoning_content") or "") + "\x00" + (m.get("content") or "")
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N) as ex:
    counts = collections.Counter(ex.map(one, range(N)))
print(f"{N} requests -> {len(counts)} distinct")
```

### Control — dense BF16, flag off then on

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \
  --served-model-name small --attention-backend flashinfer \
  --context-length 8192 --max-running-requests 64 --port 8898
```

```
32 requests -> 8 distinct
```

Adding `--enable-deterministic-inference` to the identical command:

```
32 requests -> 1 distinct
```

**The flag works on this hardware.** sm_121 is not the obstacle.

### Failing case — NVFP4 + Mamba + DFlash2

With `--enable-deterministic-inference` present and confirmed in the resolved
`ServerArgs`, temperature-0 outputs on the 27B NVFP4 checkpoint continue to vary
between identical runs.

### The failing model IS clean at batch 1, which points squarely at batch composition

Measured on the 27B NVFP4 model, **without** the flag, varying only how many of
the 32 identical requests were in flight at once:

| in flight | achieved concurrency | distinct completions from 32 identical temp-0 requests |
|---|---|---|
| 32 | 16 (server-capped) | **20** |
| 1 | 1, verified for every minute of the run | **1 — byte-identical** |

Thirty-two consecutive single-stream requests over seven minutes produced one
distinct answer. So on this checkpoint the nondeterminism is **entirely
batch-composition driven** — exactly what deterministic mode exists to remove,
and exactly what it is not removing here.

(The two rows are not a controlled A/B of batch size: the server caps achieved
concurrency, and the batch-1 run additionally required the server to be otherwise
idle. An earlier batch-1 run with unrelated traffic present returned 3 distinct.
We report that rather than omit it, but we cannot attribute those 3 — that run
lacked per-request timestamps.)

## Two notes that may save a reviewer time

**1. Validate the probe before trusting a clean result from it.** Run the
control arm *first*, flag off. If it returns 1 distinct, the probe cannot detect
nondeterminism on that model and a clean result with the flag means nothing. A
check that cannot fail proves nothing.

**2. Do not use scored benchmark items as the instrument.** We started there and
it was the wrong tool. A weak model gets every hard item wrong every time, which
scores zero flips and looks perfectly deterministic — **uniform failure is
indistinguishable from reproducibility**. Counting distinct completions is both
strictly more sensitive (one flipped token is enough) and orders of magnitude
cheaper.

## What we have not established

We have **not** isolated which of the three features is responsible. NVFP4 W4A4
kernels, the hybrid Mamba layers, and the DFlash2 acceptance path are all
plausible and all present at once in the failing configuration. Separating them
needs three bench servers we have not built. If a maintainer can say which of
those paths deterministic mode is known not to cover, that likely answers it
without the experiment.

We also have not run the concurrent-request probe against the 27B *with the flag
on* — the flag-on evidence for that model is from scored-item flips, which is
the weaker instrument described above. That run requires standing up a second
copy of the 27B, which we have queued.
